analysis.one_liner: Repeals major Affordable Care Act rules, including employer penalties and health insurer fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in a House subcommittee when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would roll back several core parts of the Affordable Care Act. It would erase the fines on large employers who do not offer health coverage, cancel the annual fee health insurers pay, and lift limits on high deductibles and on tax-free flexible spending accounts. It would also let insurers keep plan designs exempt from the law's rules even after changing benefits or cost-sharing.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers would avoid the per-worker penalties for not offering coverage and the paperwork of reporting it. Health insurers would be freed from the annual fee the ACA imposed on the industry. Higher-income households with health savings accounts and flexible spending accounts would gain bigger tax advantages, and small businesses would get more leeway in the plans they offer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large employers, insurers, and higher-income account holders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA's employer mandate, so companies with more than 50 full-time workers would no longer face fines for not offering coverage, and would no longer have to report on employee coverage to the Treasury [S2][S3].
Repeals the ACA's annual fee on health insurance entities, which the industry had lobbied against [S2][S3].

Repeals limits on annual deductibles in the small-group market and the $2,500 cap on tax-free flexible spending account contributions, and lets high-deductible plans paired with health savings accounts count as adequate coverage [S2][S3].

Lets any plan enrolled in after the ACA passed keep its 'grandfathered' exemption from the law's rules no matter how it later changes cost-sharing, employer contributions, or covered benefits [S2][S3].
Repeals the ACA provision allowing insurers to vary premiums by age beyond standard limits, and the option of low-cost catastrophic plans for people under 30 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear more of the cost if employers dropped coverage or shifted costs, since nothing would replace the requirement to offer insurance. The federal government would lose the revenue from the insurer fee and from the tax preferences expanded here, pressure that eventually falls on other taxpayers. People buying individual coverage could face plans with skimpier benefits, and repealing the age-rating provision would change how premiums are spread among younger and older enrollees.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the employer mandate removes the only firm requirement that large employers contribute to their workers' health coverage; workers whose employers drop plans would be pushed into the individual market or uninsured [S2][S3].
Letting plans keep their grandfathered exemption despite changes to cost-sharing or covered benefits could allow benefits to erode while plans avoid the ACA's consumer protections [S3].
Lifting the flexible spending account cap and expanding health savings accounts delivers the largest tax benefits to households with higher incomes that can afford to set money aside [S2].
Repealing the insurer fee and the employer penalties would remove revenue that helped offset the ACA's coverage expansion costs, adding pressure on the federal deficit [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's framing — lower premiums and more choice for small business — has a real kernel: small employers and some individuals would gain flexibility and tax room. But the largest and most certain gains go to large employers avoiding penalties and to the insurance industry avoiding its fee, while the protections removed (coverage requirements for large employers, deductible limits, benefit stability for grandfathered plans) are the ones that directly affect workers and patients. On balance the trade runs toward concentrated interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Collins of New York introduced the bill on April 15, 2013 [S1][S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Speaker sent it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and within days it was referred to the Health subcommittees of each [S5].
No further action appears in the record; it never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's target beneficiaries — large employers facing the mandate and health insurers facing the annual fee — are better off that it died, since they avoid neither now but also never faced a serious threat. Workers and patients keep the ACA protections the bill would have removed, though the bill was never close to passage in either direction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; ACA rules stayed intact

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member cosponsored, so the partisan shape beyond the Republican sponsor's affiliation never formed.

industries.note: The bill repeals the ACA's annual fee on health insurance entities and lets grandfathered plans keep their exemption even after changing benefits or cost-sharing [S2][S3]. Insurers would pay less while plans could shed benefits without losing their protected status.

Repealing the employer mandate and its reporting requirement frees large employers from fines for not offering coverage and from the cost of contributing to it; the burden shifts to workers and the individual market [S2][S3].

Repealing small-group deductible limits and the catastrophic-plan restrictions gives small employers cheaper plan options, which is the bill's stated purpose — though it comes with less protection for the employees enrolled in those plans [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Health savings account and flexible spending account holders
industries.note: The bill lets HSA-qualified high-deductible plans count as full coverage and repeals the $2,500 FSA contribution cap and OTC medicine restrictions, expanding tax-advantaged accounts — benefits that skew toward higher-income households who can afford to set money aside [S2][S3].
